issues.legal_issue: A court cannot use its inherent jurisdiction to review an appealable remand order after an aggrieved party failed to appeal it.
material_facts: The first appellate court made a remand order under Order 41, rule 23, of the Code of Civil Procedure.
The order was appealable, but no appeal was filed against it.
The High Court later reconsidered the correctness of the remand order by invoking its inherent power.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not review the remand order: section 105(2) precluded disputing its correctness, and section 151 could not be used to exercise appellate power or bypass a remedy provided by the Code.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 105(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, a party who does not appeal an appealable remand order is thereafter precluded from disputing its correctness. Sections 151 and 105(2), read with Order 41, rule 23, and Order 43, do not permit inherent jurisdiction to override a specific procedure in the Code or to function as appellate jurisdiction.

rule.if: civil_proceeding_with_remand_order and remand_order_appealable and aggrieved_party_did_not_appeal and later_court_reexamined_order_under_inherent_power

predicates.civil_proceeding_with_remand_order: A civil court proceeding included an order remanding the case for further decision.
predicates.remand_order_appealable: The remand order could be challenged by an appeal under the applicable procedure.
predicates.aggrieved_party_did_not_appeal: A party aggrieved by the remand order did not appeal it.
predicates.later_court_reexamined_order_under_inher: A later court reconsidered the correctness of the remand order by invoking its inherent power.

issues.definition: When an appealable remand order in a civil proceeding is not appealed by an aggrieved party, a later court cannot reconsider its correctness by invoking inherent power.

issues.legal_issue: Vesting of property in the state under an abolition law does not necessarily extinguish a former holder’s interest in establishing ownership at vesting and obtaining statutory compensation.
material_facts: The suit properties vested in the State under the Jagir Abolition Act while the suit was pending.
The claimant asserted that he owned the properties when the Act came into force.
It was conceded that, if the claimant’s ownership at that time were proved, he would be entitled to compensation under the Act.
The State had not been joined, and the courts had not finally determined the rights of all interested parties.
issues.conclusion: The claimant had not necessarily lost all rights in the properties, because proof of ownership when the Act came into force could entitle him to compensation. The State should be joined and the rights of all parties determined.
issues.legal_principle: The Jagir Abolition Act vested the properties in the State but provided compensation to a person proved to have owned them when the Act came into force. Applying Himatrao v. Jaikishandas and Others, [1963] 3 S.C.R. 815, the Court held that the claimant’s possible compensation interest warranted determination of the parties’ rights after the State was impleaded.

predicates.property_vested_in_state_under_abolition: Property held by a claimant vested in the State under a law abolishing the claimant’s former property-holding arrangement.
predicates.claimant_asserted_ownership_at_vesting: The claimant asserted that they owned the property when the vesting took effect.
predicates.compensation_available_if_ownership_prov: The applicable law provided compensation if the claimant’s ownership at vesting were proved.
predicates.state_not_joined_for_final_determination: The State had not been joined before the rights concerning the vested property were finally determined.

issues.definition: When property vests in the State, the claimant asserts ownership at vesting, compensation depends on proving that ownership, and the State has not been joined, the State must be joined and all parties’ rights determined.
